sections.h2: What kind of county is Johnson County, Missouri?
sections.html:
Johnson County lies in western Missouri with Warrensburg as its seat and largest city. It spans roughly 829 square miles of land and borders Lafayette, Pettis, Henry, Cass and Jackson counties. Warrensburg anchors a micropolitan area that belongs to the larger Kansas City combined statistical area (Wikipedia).

Holden and Knob Noster are the other cities. Centerview, Leeton, Chilhowee and Kingsville are villages, and Whiteman Air Force Base sits beside Knob Noster. The University of Central Missouri is in Warrensburg. Seven public districts serve the county: Warrensburg R-VI, Holden R-III, Knob Noster R-VIII, Johnson County R-VII, Leeton R-X, Kingsville R-I and Chilhowee R-IV.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts put the 2025 population at 56,670, up 4.9% from the 2020 base. Owners occupy 63.5% of homes, so renters make up a bigger slice than in most Missouri counties around Kansas City. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $235,700 and median gross rent is $932.

sections.h2: Which Johnson County offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
The county splits the work in three, as its Assessor page explains. The Assessor sets value and updates ownership on the roll, the taxing districts set rates, and the Collector prepares bills, takes payment and passes the money to the districts.

  • Assessor: Johnson County South Annex, 1310 S Maguire St, Suite B, Warrensburg, MO 64093. Phone 660-747-9822.
  • Collector: 1310 S Maguire St, Suite A, Warrensburg, MO 64093. Phone 660-747-5531.
  • Closure: county administrative offices are closed Thursday and Friday, November 26 and 27, 2026, for Thanksgiving.

The Assessor is not responsible for rates, collection or the distribution of money to schools and fire districts. A question about why a levy rose belongs with the district that levies it.

sections.h2: How does Johnson County turn market value into a tax bill?
sections.html:
The county publishes the formula. Market value is multiplied by an adjustment factor to get assessed value, then divided by 100 and multiplied by each district's rate, and the results are added up.

Johnson County assessment factors (Collector, Tax Entities and Rates page)
ClassFactor
Residential19%
Commercial32%
Agricultural12%

The county's worked example uses an assessed value of 21,903 and a combined rate of 7.6697 per $100, which gives $1,679.90. Your own rate depends on the school, fire, ambulance and city districts around your parcel.

Real estate is reassessed in odd-numbered years, and 2027 is next. An owner gets a Change in Assessed Value Notice by mail, typically in June, when assessed value rises by $500 or more, and a notice can arrive in an even year too. It carries no tax estimate. Call the Assessor for one.

sections.h2: What can a Johnson County owner do about a value they dispute?
sections.html:
The county lays out three steps. Check the notice for factual errors, then book an informal hearing with the Assessor if you have evidence of a different value or a data mistake, then file a Property Assessment Appeal Form for a Board of Equalization hearing if the informal talk fails. Hearings run by appointment, and the contact details sit on every mailed notice.

The State Tax Commission's guide says the Board of Equalization filing must be made by the second Monday in July, which will be July 12, 2027. Ask the Assessor or County Clerk for the exact form and office, and for any extension the board grants. A Board decision can go on to the Commission within 30 days of the decision letter.

  • You may owe tax while an appeal is open. Unpaid tax after December 31 draws interest and penalties.
  • Signing a value agreement with the Assessor during a Board appeal makes the matter final, and no State Tax Commission appeal follows.
  • An LLC, trust, estate or corporation must use an attorney for a State Tax Commission appeal.

sections.h2: When does Johnson County property tax come due?
sections.html:
Bills are mailed in late October and become delinquent after December 31. The Collector's FAQ says payments must carry a postmark of December 31 or earlier. A payment postmarked after that date is returned unprocessed unless the late fees are included.

You can check what you owe on the county's Search Taxes page by choosing Real Estate and entering a name, physical address or mailing address. The first number shown is the parcel number. Missouri statute 140.100 sets an 18 percent penalty on each year's delinquency for land in the back tax book, so a lapsed bill grows quickly (RSMo 140.100).

Escrowed owners get their updated tax figures through the mortgage company, though the county reminds them that timely payment still rests with the taxpayer.

sections.h2: Is there senior property tax relief in Johnson County?
sections.html:
Yes. On March 17, 2025 the County Commission passed Ordinance 25-01, which created a Senior Real Estate Tax Credit under section 137.1050. Homeowners 62 and older may qualify for a credit on the primary residence, calculated from tax increases after a starting credit year.

  • The 2026 application window ran April 1 to June 30, 2026 and has closed. Ask the Collector when the next one opens.
  • The credit does not apply to agricultural or commercial property, personal property, voter-approved bond levies or the State Blind Pension levy.
  • All taxes on the homestead must be current to qualify.
  • It does not freeze value, and reassessments continue in odd years.

Sellers should note that the credit does not move with the owner. It stays with the applicant, does not pass to a buyer, and a seller who buys elsewhere must file a new application to set a new starting year.

sections.h2: What happens if Johnson County taxes stay unpaid for years?
sections.html:
Real estate with three years of delinquent tax must be offered at the annual tax certificate sale, held on the fourth Monday in August. The 2026 sale took place on August 24 at 10 a.m. in Warrensburg. Lists run in a local newspaper for three weeks before the sale.

The buyer purchases a tax lien, not ownership. The owner of record, or anyone with a recorded lien or deed of trust on the property, can redeem for one year and afterward until a collector's deed is issued. Redemption costs the bid amount plus 10% annual interest, and 8% on any later years' tax the buyer paid. A buyer who fails to get a collector's deed within 18 months of the sale loses the lien.

Any bid above the opening amount is held as surplus. It goes to the County Treasurer, and an owner or lienholder must file a claim with the county commission within ninety days after redemption ends, or the money goes to the schools.

sections.h2: How do property taxes affect a Johnson County house sale?
sections.html: The title company pays tax due at closing, so a lapsed year does not stop a sale. Ask the Collector at 660-747-5531 for a payoff that includes penalty and interest, and order it before listing if the house is more than one year behind. A house near the three-year line is the situation to resolve first, because it can reach the August sale.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Johnson County real estate tax?
faqs.a: At the Collector's office, 1310 S Maguire St, Suite A in Warrensburg, or through the county's online payment link. The phone number is 660-747-5531. A mailed payment needs a December 31 postmark.

faqs.q: What is the Johnson County residential assessment rate?
faqs.a: Nineteen percent of market value. Commercial property is 32% and agricultural property 12%. Rates per $100 then come from the districts covering your parcel.

faqs.q: When will Johnson County reassess my house again?
faqs.a: In 2027, since Missouri reassesses real estate in odd-numbered years. A notice goes out by mail, typically in June, if the assessed value rises by $500 or more.

faqs.q: Does the Johnson County senior tax credit pass to the buyer?
faqs.a: No. It stays with the applicant. A buyer who is 62 or older would need a new application, and a seller who moves must apply again for the new home.

faqs.q: How long before Johnson County sells a home for unpaid tax?
faqs.a: A parcel with three years of delinquent tax must be offered at the sale on the fourth Monday in August. The owner can redeem during the following year by paying the bid plus 10% annual interest.
